utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As I mentioned at the outset, my opening comments will be brief and to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: In my respectful submission, at the end of the day, this is a relatively straightforward case. The order in lieu of indictment sets out clearly what the facts in issue are, and, at the outset, I'd like to describe, in my respectful submission, what the case is about and, correspondingly, what it's not about. The case is about four key issues, four central points. With respect to the book in question, "Paix et Chatiment," whether or not the book disclosed confidential information; in other words, the actus reus of the offence of contempt of the Tribunal. And, secondly, again in relation to the book, whether what's often referred to as the fault requirement or the mens rea, the knowing or mental element of the offence, is demonstrated in relation to that book. The third and fourth points relate to the article in question, the Bosnian Institute article, and it's essentially the same thing : Was there an improper disclosure of confidential information, the actus reus, and was it done knowingly, willfully, the mens rea or the fault requirement. Those are the four issues. And it's my respectful submission, and throughout the course of the trial, I'll be urging the Chamber to ensure we're focusing on those four issues, because at the end of the trial, in my respectful submission, the decisions concerning those four points will be dispositive. Now, what is the case not about, because in a case like this it's very easy to be side-tracked, it's very easy to take off-ramps that will take us into a zone that's completely irrelevant and will have the effect of clouding the issues defined in the order in lieu of indictment. This case is not about the terrible conflict that occurred in the former Yugoslavia. It's not about the atrocities that occurred in that area. It's not about who is to blame in that conflict. It's not about the politics in the region. It's not about whether the accused, Florence Hartmann, received any special treatment as a result of being a former employee of this Tribunal. It's not about that at all or, correspondingly, whether she's entitled to differential treatment as a result of being a journalist. In my respectful submission, the case is not about that. It's not about what the media are saying or have been saying about the case, and it's not about individuals' opinions about the fact that the accused has been charged. At the end of the evidence, I anticipate it will demonstrate -- the case will demonstrate that the steps taken by the accused and the words that she used and the comments that she used in her publications were not mere inadvertence, they were not an accident; they were deliberate. I anticipate that the evidence will demonstrate that her own words, which are what are at issue here, in essence, were a statement of defiance. And if the evidence does demonstrate that, in my respectful submission, at the end of the day, this case is all about one of accountability. The focus in this case will be on her own words, not what someone else did, not what anybody involved in these proceedings did or did not do. It will turn on her own words, what she decided to publish. And I expect that at the end of the trial, the issue will not be so much the actus reus on either of the publications, because that, for all intents and purposes, is not an issue. The issue will be one of mens rea, whether or not she, in fact, knew what she was doing, whether it was willful, whether it was knowing. I anticipate that the evidence throughout the trial and at the end of the trial will demonstrate that in the affirmative. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacFarlane. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: My learned friend has emphasised, quite rightly, that it is imperative that Your Honours do not get side-tracked in this case. The Defence has no fear on that account. Your Honours have had the privilege of sitting in judgement in many cases in this institution for many years of far greater complexity than this particular matter. There is no danger whatsoever of getting side-tracked with a Bench of this experience. But what my learned friend states, and I would agree with him, is that one should also focus on the words of my client, Ms. Hartmann. It is my respectful submission that is precisely what my learned friend singularly failed to do in his previous incarnation as the amicus investigator in this case. Your Honour, what are the words of my client that may be relevant? Well, Your Honour, let me start by citing her interview on the 22nd of May, 2008, in which she stated: "I am extremely surprised and devastated by these proceedings by the Tribunal. I have worked for years without counting all the time I invested to serve the Tribunal, to the detriment of my family and my children, and I carried out my work such that no one could ever doubt my commitment, which certainly went beyond that demanded by my employer, the United Nations, and with the intellectual rigour recognised by many observers." Your Honour, she continued, and this is page 4 out of 10 of that interview: "If I may continue on my career," she says, "I formally reject having ever knowingly violated any regulation and affirm that I never knowingly or willingly endeavoured to hamper the course of justice in any way." Your Honour, I'll read just one more paragraph. She continues: "I note that much of the information contained in the pages of my book, i.e., the documents mentioned in the file, communicated to my adviser, Maitre Bourdon up to the start of the interview, had been disclosed. Much of this information had been available, some of it for years now, without ever giving rise to my reactions by the Tribunal." And then she quotes many, many documents. Your Honour, my learned friend has come very late in the day to the importance of the words of my client, because as you'll see from the face of this interview, the documents my client referred to, the details my client referred to, were not even translated to my learned friend. They were not put to the previous specially-appointed Trial Chamber. They were not part of his report. Your Honour, there's no fault, in my respectful submission, or no doubt is cast on the integrity and impartiality and highest professionalism of the originally-constituted, specially-appointed Trial Chamber. They were handicapped, due to no fault of their own, by a completely incomplete dossier and report that was produced by my learned friend in his previous incarnation as the amicus investigator of this case. None of these facts were put before Your Honours 'colleagues previously. Your Honour, let's be clear. The two confidential decisions that are the subject matter of these proceedings were never read by my client at the time she was working as the spokesperson of the former Prosecutor, Carla Del Ponte. Indeed, the first time that they were read were when they were handed to her by my learned friend sitting opposite. And that is not an assertion, that is an issue where the parties are in agreement. And, Your Honours, I will refer you to the 7th of February agreed facts, where my learned friend consents and agrees that that is the truth. Your Honour, Ms. Hartmann was never briefed while she was a spokesperson of the Prosecutor in relation to any of these decisions. She never spoke to the press, there's no briefing she gave in relation to those decisions, and there is no evidence that my learned friend intends to put before you to controvert these assertions. Your Honour, it's also important, in the Defence's respectful submission, to note that in relation to the second decision, the 6th of April decision, it was rendered three days after -- three days after my client left her job as the spokesperson of the Prosecutor. Again, this is not a matter of controversy. This is an agreed fact, and it is set down in the 6th of February, 2009 filing. She left her job as spokeswoman on the 3rd of April of that year. So, Your Honour, this case is not about abuse of position of trust. This is not about an evil individual who is somehow trying to hamper the administration of justice, get a false result due to witness intimidation, as have been most of the contempt cases that this Court has heard. My learned friend accepts, once again, in his 7th of February, 2009, filing, that my client did not act with reprehensible motives. Your Honour, by the end of this case, we will ask you to step back and review, as you would do in any event, the evidence in its totality, and it will be our strong -- the respectful submission that a striking feature of this case has been the constant erosion in my learned friend's case. From the time he submitted his first report, the case has eroded as far as the allegations are concerned in material particulars to the pre-trial brief. And again since the pre-trial brief has been filed and again in some particulars, there has been a stepping back by my learned friend for the Prosecution. Your Honours, by the end of the case, it is the Defence's respectful submission and belief that Your Honours will find that my learned friend has not discharged his heavy responsibility to prove this criminal matter to the required standard of beyond reasonable doubt. Now, Your Honours, in assessing the parameters of this case, it is, of course, apt to bear in mind that the crime of contempt is not a strict liability offence. It is not any technical breach of a confidential order that would give rise to responsibility. And, Your Honours, we say, on behalf of Ms. Hartmann, that when one dissects the Prosecution's case, four facts are asserted which it is said that my client breached: namely, the existence -- this is the first fact, the existence of the confidential decisions; the fact that those decisions were confidential; the identity of the moving party; and, fourthly, the subject, namely, that the protective measures were granted in relation to documents. Your Honour, Mr. President, all these facts will be shown to have been public. Now, the Defence do not say -- it is not such a crude argument to say that any breach of confidentiality gives a license to anyone to publish with abandon so as to prejudice the proper administration of justice; not a bit of it. But we do say -- and we do not say that any journalist can unilaterally arrogate to themselves the seat of moral judgement to decide what the public should or should not know. We fully accept that these decisions are for Your Honours, who make judicial determinations. But what we do say is that this Tribunal, Judges of this Court, made these facts public themselves. Your Honours, we will prove, from public filings, that brother Judges and sister Judges of this Court made the existence of these two confidential decisions public; in particular, the fact that the decision were made, the identity of the moving party, the confidential character of those decisions, that the focus of those decisions had to do with national interest. And, Your Honour, we will refer in due course to the Milutinovic decision by the Appeals Chamber in 2006. There's decisions in 2007. There's the Milosevic Trial Chamber decision of 2004, where the factual matrix was made public by the Judges. But what is the Defence argument in that case? The Defence argument is unequivocal. It is that the Tribunal and the Judges of this Court have the power to amend confidentiality orders, but the Rules do not dictate any form by which confidentiality orders need to be lifted; and it is not so mathematical a formula that every confidential decision requires a formal decision of the Bench to render it public. It is our respectful submission that by the end of this case, Your Honours will be satisfied that the Tribunal, by actus contrarius, may decide to lift the confidential nature of a decision, in whole or in material particulars. Your Honours, that, in fact, is borne out by Your Honour himself, Judge Moloto. If one looks at the decision of this case itself -- the history of this case itself, one would, perhaps, remember that on the 19th of May, 2009, Your Honours rendered a confidential decision pertaining to a Defence motion for leave to appeal against a decision relating to the binding order request that we put towards the Registry. Now, Your Honour, that decision, its existence, and its subject matter, were confidential. There's no dispute about that. But, Your Honour, Mr. President, during the Status Conference of that day, after the decision was made public, Your Honour referred to the existence of that decision, including the subject matter, including the purported effect, and the fact that it was confidential, and Your Honour did that in public session. Now, there is absolutely no suggestion that that was improper or that any Rule has been violated. Instead, what the Defence submit is that this, even in this small case, is evidence that the confidential nature as to the existence of the decision and its status could be lifted by Your Honour, acting in a judicial capacity to act as a waiver or a lifting to the extent that Your Honour has made facts public. Now, this is an important part of the Defence case, as you will hear. Your Honour, when assessing -- and before I move on there, contrary to what my learned friend has opined, this goes directly to the actus reus of the offence, the actus reus is very much in issue. It's very much in issue, we say, because the Tribunal, acting actus contrarius, lifted confidentiality to the extent that is asserted to be criminal, when done by my client, there is simply no actus reus. So actus reus is in dispute unequivocally. And, indeed, as my learned friend should know, he has the pre-trial brief, we've made it clear that unless there's a clear waiver, every aspect of the case is in issue, unless expressly agreed, and we put the Prosecution to strict proof on all aspects, including most fundamentally and basically actus reus and mens rea. Your Honour, the other point is: It is germane to note that the applicant, the person who -- the country, the state, that sought the protections themselves have waived that confidentiality. How perverse would it be, in the Defence respectful submission, that the applicant who requests confidentiality can go 'round talking about the same facts, and yet a journalist who repeats those facts should be held criminally responsible? Your Honour, in public session, in the International Court of Justice, of course, one of the principal organs of the United Nations, the representative of Serbia and Montenegro said publicly, on the 8th of May, 2006, in the genocide case, and I quote: "Madam President," and at that time it was Judge Rosalyn Higgins, "Madam President, with all due respect to this honourable Court, the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro are not entitled to discuss the contents of the redacted sections of the Supreme Defence Council documents for two serious reasons." Your Honour, with your leave, I pause there. It's important to note contents are mentioned, as opposed to what we say are the legal reasoning and the decisions of a Bench. And, Your Honour, he states, the representative, one -- is the two reasons: The redacted sections were classified by the Supreme Defence Council as a military secret, and according to the confidential decision to the Council of Ministers of Serbian Montenegro, as a matter of national security interest; and, 2: "At this moment the redacted sections of the STC documents are under protective measures imposed by the ICTY confidential order, and we are obliged to respect that order." But, Your Honour, what's important to note is that the applicant did not seek protective measures, nor was he granted -- nor was the state granted, by their own understanding, protective measures in relation to: firstly, the fact that the state, Serbia and Montenegro, as it then was, had applied for protective measures in relation to those documents; secondly, that they were the applicant; thirdly, the reasons for the application; and, fourthly, the fact that should measures be granted, the existence of those measures remain confidential. Your Honour, therefore, none of these matters, in our respectful submission, when you look at this case in the 'round can be said to have been germane to the confidential order or the confidential part of the decision of the Appeals Chambers that rendered these decisions originally. Now, Your Honour, when one goes to mens rea, the public nature of the decisions is relevant. This is not a statement of defiance, as my learned friend fears. This is a matter of intent. Six months before my client's book was published, two world-widely -- globally distributed newspapers, "The New York Times" and the "International Herald Tribune," on the 9th of April, 2007, had displayed articles -- written articles quoting exactly the same facts that are included in my client's book, and not a whisper -- not a murmur was heard from the corridors of this Court to say that "The New York Times" or the powerful "International Herald Tribune" had acted in breach of contempt. Now, Your Honours, this is different from the Haxhiu case we will show. It's different from an argument that there's a public secret. This is relevant to mens rea. The fact that two of the highest-profile newspapers in the world have talked about and discussed and critiqued the very decisions that my client, as a journalist, later wrote about, is relevant to her intent, her belief that she was willfully or knowingly interfering in any way with the proper administration of justice. Your Honour, an important feature of distinction, and we'll come to this at the end in closing, is when one surveys the jurisprudence of this Court, the Haxhiu cases and the other cases, one of the features are the Tribunal is very prompt in acting after, for example, a witness's name was made public. This case can be distinguished in many, many ways from that. Your Honour, for six months, no murmur. My client's belief that what she did was lawful and proper and unremarkable, has been and will be established by the Defence, and it is the Defence's strong belief that my learned friend will be shown to have singularly failed in his responsibility to prove a guilty mind, as it is his burden to do. Your Honour, similarly, even earlier than that, on the 9th of March, 2007, the Institute of War and Peace Reporting had submitted a detailed article, again, almost duplicating the areas that my client is now asserted to have written about in criminal violation of her responsibilities to the Court. Your Honour, the same argument applies in relation to that. And, Your Honour, that's at 2 and 3 of our 65 ter list, tab 2 and 3 of or 65 ter list. Before I move on, I will -- it is important to bear in mind that even back in 2005, the 17th of May, 2005, albeit before the Appeals Chamber gave its orders, there was a very extensive special investigation by the Institute of War and Peace Reporting, very extensive report at tab 14, in which all these matters were discussed and made public. Your Honour, it is, therefore, our -- it will be our submission that the mens rea aspect has not been proved. Your Honour, as far as special privileges for journalists are concerned, the matter is not straight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I remind you, Mr. Khan, we are not in closing argument, but in opening statement. Nothing has been proved, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You were, when one is reviewing the Prosecution's case, it must be viewed through the prism, in the Defence's respectful submission, that this Court, established as it was to uphold the highest standards of international justice, will view the accumulated years of jurisprudence from other international and regional courts and bodies carefully and view those cases as lending persuasive weight that will inform Your Honours' exercise of discretion. In order to convict my client, my learned friend will have to persuade Your Honours to set aside decades of jurisprudence from the European Court of Human Rights. Your Honour, there are cases of Webber -- there's the "Sunday Times" case known as the thalidimide case, there is "The Observer" newspaper case, the spy-catcher case. All these cases -- Strasbourg was clear. It said that in deciding whether or not a restriction in the form of contempt served a legitimate objective or was proportionate, one must look at several factors that we'll come to in the closing brief, but, Your Honours, they include the right of journalistic -- journalists to write as the watch-dog of society in democratic pluralistic societies, and that's the watch-dog, not only the executive, but all parts, including the judiciary and the legislature. That's the first link. But the second is the public's right to know. And, Your Honour, it is our submission that when one bears in mind that the offence of contempt does not appear in the Statute of this Court, but falls within your implied powers, your inherent jurisdiction, in order to fulfill your overall mandate, it is critical not to overly extend the envelope, not to overly extend the parameters of criminal responsibility, so that they would stymie -- they would stymie freedom of speech that is needed. Your Honour, in short, every aspect of the Prosecution's case will fall away. The witnesses that we will call, Natasa Kandic, Mr. Joinet, will -- and Nura Alispahic, will demonstrate both the margin of deference that is given under international human rights norms to journalistic freedom -- although it's a qualified right, the European -- the Strasbourg cases that we will refer to are almost on all fours with the offence that is charged against our client. And, Your Honour, when one is looking and critiquing my learned friend's case, we would ask you not to be -- not to turn away from that jurisprudence. We are confident that you will not. And if you do not, our client will be acquitted. Your Honours, those are my submissions in opening, and I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Khan. Just before you call your witness, Mr. MacFarlane, you had raised an issue earlier, and I don't think we did finally dispose of it, your position as an intended witness for the Defence. I just wanted to say to you that Mr. Khan indicated the number of witnesses that he's going to call, and he's now indicated he's calling three and you're not one of those. Does that dispose of your situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may call your witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that you're employed by a company located in Paris called Flammarion.

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, I work for Flammarion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I do apologise. Your Honours, perhaps before we move -- the witness hasn't given his name, and I do note at page 27, line 2, this witness is identified as Mr. Robin Vincent, and, of course, that is patently wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Could you state your full name to the Court, to the Tribunal, please?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: My name is Kermarrec and my name is Yorric. Do you want to know when I was born? I was born on November the 12th, 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe if you would spell your name for us so that we can write it down, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] K-e-r-m-a-r-r-e-c;-r-r-e-c, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the surname. What's the first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my surname. My first name is Y-o-r -r-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. MacFarlane, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that you are employed with an organisation, a company known as Flammarion at Paris.

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: I work for Flammarion, the headquarters of Flammarion being in Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Can you describe the nature of the business?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Flammarion is a publishing company, distributing books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Can you describe the company in terms of its size?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Flammarion is the fifth French publisher, general publisher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Can you advise the Chamber of your position -- your title within the organisation?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: I mainly deal with legal issues for Flammarion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I understand that in 2006, late 2006, Flammarion entered into discussions with the accused before this Chamber, with a view to the prospects of publishing a book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Did those discussions lead to the signing of a publishing agreement?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, the discussions led to the signing of a publishing agreement in December 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The precise date was ...

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: The precise date was December the 20th, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: What was the name of the proposed book at that stage?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: The name in the contract was the following "Dans les coulisses du Tribunal de La Haye."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And I understand that that subsequently changed on publication to another name?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, correct, the present title being "Paix et Chatiment," "Peace and Punishment."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Were there any other persons that signed the contract or were involved in the discussions, or was the accused the sole author?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Well, there are two questions in your question. I believe that there was an agent involved in the discussions focusing on this contract, that Florence had an agent, but Florence Hartmann is the only -- the sole author of this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The contract which has been tendered before this Chamber notes the prospect of an advance, that is, a financial advance, which could be provided by Flammarion in respect of the book. Can you advise as to whether or not an advance was, in fact, provided?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. The advance payment, as mentioned in the contract, was paid to Florence Hartmann. The first half was paid when the contract was signed, and the second half was paid when the book was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. And as I understand it, under this publishing agreement there was a royalty agreement; that is to say, it was contemplated that a certain amount of the monies paid for the book would then be provided to the author by way of royalties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Can you advise the Chamber with respect to the level or number of sales of this book up to date or the most recent figures that you have?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: On June the 8th, some 3.799 books have been sold.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Is the book still actively being sold by Flammarion?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, the book is still being sold.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Can you comment with respect to any sales or any other editions in other countries? That is to say, did Flammarion have rights for other editions in other languages in other countries or not?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Flammarion only has rights for French editions, and translation rights in other countries belong to Ms. Hartmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. MacFarlane. Yes, Mr. Khan, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Bon jour, Mr. Kermarrec. Your Honours, before we start, we have a number of binders, of documents, which we intend to use in cross-examination of Mr. Kermarrec and in cross-examination of Mr. Vincent, and with the assistance of the Court usher, we'll have those distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: There is a copy for each of Judges, for the Registry, for our friend for the Prosecution, and for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you very much, for that, and my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Kermarrec, you discussed a moment ago with the Prosecutor the process of negotiation of a publishing agreement between yourself, Flammarion, and Ms. Hartmann. Were you a party to these negotiation?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you indicate, perhaps, who, on behalf of Flammarion, was responsible for those?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: This was the responsibility of Gilles Haeri.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And any other person at Flammarion who dealt with Ms. Hartmann in relation to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: You have the direct publisher of Florence Hartmann, [indiscernible], who has followed the publishing process.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you explain, perhaps briefly, why Flammarion was of the view that it should -- or that it was interested in publishing Ms. Hartmann's book? Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Florence Hartmann was, before the negotiations, one of the experts in international issues for Flammarion, and also she was -- she knew about all the questions concerning Serbia. She had been a journalist working for "Le Monde." She had followed all these cases. She had published a book in 1999 on Milosevic, and she also acted as a spokeswoman to Carla Del Ponte; and this is the reason why we wanted to publish her book.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And did you, and by "you,"I mean Flammarion, do you think it would be of publish interests for a book of this sort that you and Ms. Hartmann were negotiating about?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, since there was a very strong political discussion on the -- on international justice and the genocide in former Yugoslavia. Therefore, it is obvious that for us, this was of public interest [as interpreted], it was of very strong publish interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. And simply for the transcript, at page 31, line 25, it should be "of public interests." In general terms, Mr. Kermarrec, are the books published and produced by Flammarion protected by the freedom of expression?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, all the books are protected by the freedom of expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you indicate a convenient moment where we could take a break. [Microphone not activated] If it is a convenient moment for you, but if it is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, any moment convenient to Your Honours would be convenient to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We usually take a break at quarter past. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Kermarrec, before the break I was asking you questions as to whether the books published by Flammarion were covered by the principle of freedom of expression, and you indicated that this was the case. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And may I take it, perhaps, that this would be the case with the book published by Ms. Hartmann; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might rise at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I think we have a fundamental question that we need to deal with at this point, and I would like to raise it, and that is that the witness has been put forward as a fact witness, not as an expert, and we seem to be moving more and more in the direction of freedom of expression, whether the book in question is covered by notions of freedom of expression, whether Flammarion -- what Flammarion's view is on that. It seems to me that those are all issues for the Chamber to consider in due course and are in the realm of issues of law, so I am concerned that we're moving in a direction that's inappropriate, and I thought I should raise it at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you wish me to respond or should I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course you have to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, I can reassure the Chamber that I'm not going to ask Mr. Kermarrec to draw any expertise -- any type of expertise that he may or may not have, nor am I seeking from him any legal conclusion that the Chamber might be minded to make or not to make at the end of this case. What I'm seeking from this witness is the confirmation of a number of facts that pertain to his work as a legal adviser to Flammarion. This is the reason why he was called in the first place. There were persons at Flammarion who might be factually relevant to this case, Your Honour, who had taken part in this negotiation. These people were not called. This person was called as the director of Flammarion. This is the person that has been called and the reason why he was called. I'm asking him questions that pertain to the course of his work, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As long as you stay in the fact part and not move into expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could you indicate, perhaps, to complement the answer that you've given a moment ago, why it is important from the point of view of a publisher, like yours, Flammarion, that your publications be protected by the principle of freedom of expression? Could you explain briefly why that is important and relevant to you?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: The freedom of expression for a publisher is really the core of his activity, particularly for books -- for political books, or for books in dispute, or books carrying certain opinions, and a publisher -- and that this is a private service, because if they are disputed, concerning the content of the books, they will no more be able to continue their job, and the political stake is very important; and the publisher might be placed in a position not to be able to publish books or to allow people to express opinions concerning political issues or issues of general interest. This is the reason why publishers really try to support authors giving very strong political opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who does this protection protect, sir? Does it protect you, as the publisher, or does it protect the author, because your answer is not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The freedom of expression protects the publisher and the author, and they both do a common job, carry out the job jointly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Mr. Kermarrec, and I'll give you the warning that counsel generally receives. We'll ask you to slow down a bit for the interpreters and the transcript, so they can follow your words and translate them for the benefits of counsel and the rest of the people in the courtroom. You've also been asked about the sales of Ms. Hartmann's book by my colleague. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall perhaps indicating, I believe, that 3.799 copies had been sold of this book, as of 8th of June, 2009? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you were also asked by my colleague about what in English would be referred as an advance, and I think the contract refers to the French, "delavois [phoen]." Could you explain briefly what that means in publishing terms?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: The advance paid to the author is an advance on royalties and copyrights, and this means that the advance is compensated by the author's publishing rights, which are paid for by royalties, and the publisher starts paying the copyrights after the publication. Once the advance has been paid by the copyrights, are such royalties or percentages paid on sales.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So perhaps to make that a little bit clearer for the Court, Mr. Kermarrec, am I to understand that, in effect, you, Flammarion, paid an advance of 15.000 Euro to Ms. Hartmann. And as the royalties, as you call them, come in at Flammarion, these royalties are actually cashed in by Flammarion and are deducted from the 15.000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, the royalties have been deducted from the 15.000 Euros.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps because my question was not the clearest, is that correct that the royalties do not come on top of the 15.000, but they actually are paid only as of the moment when more than 15.000 Euro have been made in royalties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And one may also add that to -- that the advance is not compensated by the sales of this book, which means that Ms. Hartmann's account in Flammarion is in the red.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 15.000, do I understand, from the royalties, not the royalties from the 15.000?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I can perhaps try to make it clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can you tell this Chamber, Mr. Kermarrec, how much royalties have been cashed in at this point by Ms. Hartmann, approximately?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: I'll try to explain that once again. We have paid, all in all, 15.000 Euros, which -- 15.000 Euros are an advance on the copyrights to be paid. Given the sales of the book, i.e., 3.799 books, I believe that the royalties amount to 5.000 Euros. Today, the copyright of Ms. Hartmann is in the red for an amount of 10.000 Euros, which means that the future sales will come and reduce this minus -- this 15.000 Euros. Once the 15.000 Euros are completely compensated, Ms. Hartmann will be able to get a new amount from Flammarion.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I think you've said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, if I may just ask you, from my interpretation I keep hearing reference to copyright, and if you could just clear that. Copyright and royalties to me are two distinct issues, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour. I can indicate from the French word that Mr. Kermarrec is using of royalties, this is the entitlement to which Ms. Hartmann is entitled as of the contract which pertains to the copyrights that are indicated in the agreement. This is effectively the money she receives from the sales and for each individual sales on the book. The copyright in English, as you said, is not quite accurate in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But may I clarify, perhaps, Mr. Kermarrec, with you, and I think you've said it, but at this stage would it be correct to suggest that Ms. Hartmann is actually in debt, vis-a-vis Flammarion, for approximately 10.000 Euro? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps to clear this issue, is that information which at any stage you communicated to the Prosecutor, Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you've indicated, I believe, to my colleague that the book continues to sell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, the book is still on sale, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And are you aware of any effort or any request on the part of the Prosecution to stop or prevent the sale of this book? Are you aware of any such effort on his part?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You've also discussed the process of negotiation that took place between Ms. Hartmann and your company, Flammarion. I would like to ask you this: At the time when you entered into an agreement with Ms. Hartmann, did you know of Ms. Hartmann as a trustworthy and reliable author?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Given her records, her resume, and since she had been working as a journalist for one of the largest French newspapers, we considered her experience to consider that she was an author trustworthy to be reliable that could be published by Flammarion.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And was her journalistic experience and her journalistic reputation at all relevant to your decision to enter into an agreement with her?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that in view of the fact that you, Flammarion, decided to publish Ms. Hartmann's book, you were satisfied with the journalistic work, the quality of the book that had been produced by Ms. Hartmann; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, we feel that, in Flammarion, that this is a book of a certain quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you have any reason to believe, Mr. Kermarrec, that the book contained anything that is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you have any reason to believe that it contains anything false or untrue?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to believe that Ms. Hartmann wrote that book in anything other than plain good faith?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And at the time of publishing this book, did you have any reason to believe that the book contained material, which, at the time of publication, was still protected by confidential orders, the disclosure of which could have criminal consequences? Did you have any reason to believe this was the case?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you have any reason to believe that Ms. Hartmann would have tried to mislead Flammarion as to the content of her book?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so either.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in light of the good name and reputation that you've said you were aware of, the good name and reputation of Ms. Hartmann, do you have any reason to believe that Ms. Hartmann hid from her publisher, Flammarion, that the book contained contemptuous material or material that should not be discussed publicly? Do you have any reason to believe that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've asked that question, and it's been answered, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Your Honour, this is all the questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just at the stage before I call on you, Mr. MacFarlane, the point I want to make to both parties: You've been talking about an agreement and talking about a book, both of which are not in evidence yet. I don't know what's going to be the possible position with these books and these documents. You can re-examine the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. MacFarlane, it looks like Judge Guney has a question to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please help me in clarifying a point. I would like to know whether you took part in the negotiations regarding the publishing agreement or the publishing of this book?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Personally, not, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you a signatory to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: No, I'm not a signatory to this agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you followed this matter?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: I started following up this matter where -- at the point where there was some legal requests that were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And are you still involved in this matter?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, especially as a witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: My first question is in relation to the publishing agreement or contract, which is Exhibit P8 in these proceedings, and I believe you have a copy in your file as well. My question is this: There is a reference a moment ago to royalties and copyright, and possible overlap. I direct your attention to Article 5(A), which appears to make reference to copyright as a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the Prosecutor indicate perhaps what sentence he is referring to. That would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, are you able to come to the assistance of your learned friend?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. It's in the second paragraph of sub (A). In English, it reads: "If the author has not received advance payment for copyright, she shall be paid 305 Euros accordingly."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to point out -- if you allow me, I would just like to point out, if you allow me, that this article is talking about a case where the publisher would not publish the book in question. Since the book was published, this is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: As well, my learned friend, in his questions to you, asked you if you had any reason to believe that there is any inaccuracy in the book, and you indicated, "No"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: My question is this: Does Flammarion investigate whether or not there are any inaccuracies or do you rely on the author?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: We rely on the author, and the publishing house is not there to rewrite or to do a job that has been done by the author over again. The relationship between the publishing house and the author is a trusted relationship, which means that if we have any doubt or any indications, and it was not the case with Ms. Hartmann, then, of course, we could ask to double-check or we could ask for additional information from the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Similarly, my learned friend asked you whether or not you had any reason to believe that there is confidential information or inappropriate information in the book. Is your position essentially the same thing, that Flammarion doesn't actively investigate that, but rather relies on the author?

utterances.speaker: YORRIC FELIX KERMARREC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. MacFarlane. Any questions, Judge? Mr. Mettraux, I note that Judge Guney asked questions after you had finished your cross-examination. Do you have any questions arising from the questions by him?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: None, Your Honour, but I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that case, thank you very much, Mr. Kermarrec. That brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. You are now excused. You may stand down. Please travel well back home. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next witness on behalf of the Prosecution is Robin Vincent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. MacFarlane. I know that -- it has come to my notice that, in fact, these documents are already in evidence. I'm sorry about my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you sure your witness is here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I was just wondering the same thing myself. I have every reason to believe that the witness will be here. I assume he was in another part of the building and was waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, and make yourself comfortable. Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. One preliminary issue. The evidence will demonstrate that Mr. Vincent is presently the Registrar for the Special Tribunal for Lebanon. That obviously raises issues of immunity from process, and I wanted to advise the Chamber that that issue has been addressed by me, and I have provided copies of correspondence to my learned friend. The -- as a result of an exchange of correspondence, the Assistant Secretary-General for Legal Affairs, on behalf of the Secretary-General, has waived Mr. Vincent's immunity from legal process by a letter dated the 6th of January, 2009. I have a copy of that letter, if either my learned friend or the Chamber feels that it ought to be a part of the record, but my friend has a copy and has had a copy for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's of any assistance, Mr. Vincent is well known, I believe, to everybody in the courtroom, and what my learned friend has said regarding the waiver of immunity accurately portrays the situation, and the Defence is not contending or contesting that averment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. It's up to you. I don't think the Chamber necessarily wants the document to be tendered into evidence, but you decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: It seems to me that a notation on the record is sufficient, so I'm not intending to tender the letter. Thank you very much for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Mr. Vincent, I understand that you are presently the Registrar for the Special Tribunal for Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And I understand that you have previously worked within other international criminal tribunals and as well within court services in the United Kingdom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Could you briefly outline your experience in that respect?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Very briefly, yes, 39 years in the Court Service for England and Wales, following that two years, on and off, working in Russia, before the UN invited me to become the Registrar for the Special Court for Sierra Leone, where I was for three and a half years. And then subsequent to that a number of posts, again at the request of the United Nations, either at the Cambodian courts and the then various kind of undertakings, including a five-month spell here at ICTY as the acting Deputy Registrar. And then subsequently for the last two years, I've been involved in the establishment of the Special Tribunal for Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Vincent. I just have a couple of questions based on your hands-on, in-the-field experience, and they relate to the question of protective measures. Can you describe to the Chamber the most common scenarios in which protective measures are seen as necessary and the circumstances that most commonly give rise to an application for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Well, most commonly, in my experience, it's when it's the involvement of protection of the giving of evidence by witnesses. Protective measures are not infrequent; in fact, probably very much in the majority, insofar as many of the war crimes tribunals are concerned. In international jurisdiction, it happens to be less frequent, but, still again, protective measures are frequently required so far as witnesses are concerned. Since I've been involved in the international scene, then, of course, and again with my brief experience here in the Yugoslav Tribunal, but also with Sierra Leone as well, there have been occasions when, of course, protective measures, so far as confidentiality, in terms of states are concerned; or, indeed, information which is coming from outside, an individual witness or perhaps from a body or an organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I direct your attention, in particular, to the last scenario you described, and that is involving information from a state. Can you describe, for the benefit of the Chamber, your experience or your understanding with respect to the implications of the improper disclosure of state information in situations where there have been protective measures?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Well, I have to say immediately that my experience is far greater so far as protected witnesses are concerned, but I do have some experience so far as states are concerned. And putting it very, very -- I hope simply very bluntly is the fact that tribunals in the international scene, and indeed the Lebanon Tribunal, which I am involved in at the moment, faces a significant challenge in terms of the level of cooperation that these tribunals can get from states in a number of regards. And what I would say is that it's, I think, fairly obvious that if there is any lack of confidence in the tribunal, so far as the state is concerned that's in a position to provide evidence which is crucial to that particular tribunal, once its recognised that there has been or may well be dangers of breaches, then it's unlikely that the cooperation that tribunal seeks will actually be forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vincent, good morning.

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It is still the morning. Is it correct, in your experience, that there is a whole range of -- is it correct, in your experience, that a mere breach of a confidential order need not give rise to harm, to any prejudice to the administration of justice?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: I have to say I'm interested in the description of a mere breach. Have I -- do I have experience of situations where there has been, as a result of an administrative error or because perhaps the identity of a witness has become known, has there been a cataclysmic impact so far as that tribunal is concerned? No. I have experience of that, but certainly it's something which every tribunal/court, whether it's national or international, would seek to avoid. So I think every such instance of that does, in itself, have some impact. And I think if there is a situation where, for instance, a tribunal was seen from the outside world as consistently or at any stage being perhaps prone to breaches of confidentiality, I think it does have a serious impact on that organisation. But it has happened in the past with -- I certainly can think of a couple of instances where witnesses -- confidentiality of witnesses has been breached, once deliberately, I can remember in Sierra Leone, and on a couple of occasions accidentally. It doesn't actually enhance the reputation of the tribunal, and it certainly can cause difficulties for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed. And is it correct that often courts, for example, such as the Special Court for Sierra Leone, based as it is in the conflict or the former conflict zone, in those courts, as well as this Tribunal and at the Lebanon Tribunal, the issue of witness protection is the -- perhaps one of the most vexing questions that is faced regarding confidentiality; that's one of the issues that is of the most critical importance? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: I would certainly agree. Whether it's vexing, it's certainly challenging. And it's something which is crucial to that particular institution, especially if there are any concerns from those who may find themselves being asked to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, of course, the reason it is vexing or challenging is because of the most direct consequences that could take place to a witness should, for example, his or her name be revealed?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and I think the -- if I could add, is that, of course, the issue frequently is - and I mentioned Sierra Leone as one example - is if the breach of confidentiality, so far as a witness is concerned, is seen to be deliberate, then of course that's a completely, wholly different ball game to one where there is an inadvertence administrative error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. But in answer to my question, the reason why it's of most direct interest is because of the possible consequences of a breach to a human being?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Certainly, so far as witnesses are concerned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, perhaps if the witness can be shown, I think -- has the document been distributed from Sierra Leone? Just one moment. Mr. Vincent, it's not in that binder, the first document. It's a later edition. To the Judges first, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I guess before you give the witness that document, you must pass it by his learned colleague. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are copies, of course, for my learned friend, for the Registry, and for Your Honours. I hope they'll be distributed. Your Honour, if my learned friend has seen it, may the copy be handed to the witness, with your leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I am seeing it and reading it for the first time. There has not been any discussions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know what you are reading, because I've got several pages which are flagged. I am not sure which of these documents has been given to the witness or is he receiving all?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they are identical bundles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I have -- a number are flagged on the material I have, but I -- this is the first time I've seen it. I have no idea what the contents are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if my learned friend is patient, he will get to the documents in a moment. This is, of course, cross-examination. For the time being, all I'm asking is if the document that my learned friend has, if he is content, it is the same document I am seeking to show to the witness. That's the limit of what I'm seeking to do at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is the limit of my question to you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I have a document with four flags on it and a yellow sticky, and that's what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You may proceed, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm most obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vincent, if you can peruse those documents for a moment. They are very short. There's four tabs. The first, details, Rule 52 and 53 of the Special Court for Sierra Leone, Rules and Procedure of Evidence. Are you familiar with those Rules?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And at tab 2, you will see the date the 7th of March, 2003, a decision by Judge Bankole Thompson, approving the indictment and ordering non-disclosure in relation to the case against Charles Ghankay Taylor. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, no doubt, you will see at tab 2 your name, detailed as the Registrar?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you were the Registrar on the 7th of March, 2003, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And at -- you will see on the decision dated the 7th of March that His Honour Judge Thompson -- [French spoken on English channel]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Khan, suddenly we are getting the French translation through what is supposed to be an English channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps that will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Khan. Let the technical people sort it out for us. Madam Registrar? It is okay now? Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to say if it is -- if I was being translated into French, I lived in the hope that I would come across somewhat more eloquently than I do at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vincent, if you can look at, first of all, Rule 53, and if you look at paragraph B of that Rule, can you see it detailed, as a Rule for the Court of which you were the Registrar, that when approving an indictment, the designated Judge may, on application of the Prosecutor, order there be no disclosure of the indictment until it is served on the accused, or in the case of a joint accused, all of the accused? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: I do see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. And if you could turn over the page to tab 2, and that's the 7th of March decision. And on the page, the penultimate paragraph, above Judge Bankole Thompson's signature, you will see that the learned Judge, seized of that matter in that Court, ordered that the indictment, the warrant of arrest, and the transfer and detention, remain confidential until further order; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, if you can turn over the page again, you will see a press statement from the Prosecutor of the Special Court for Sierra Leone, the then Prosecutor, Mr. David Crane. Do you see that press release dated the 4th of June?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, after perusing it, that Prosecutor David Crane made public the fact that an indictment had been issued? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And the date is the 4th of June?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If you can turn the tab once more, can you see a decision of Judge Pierre Boutet, dated the 12th of June, 2003?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And that's an order for the disclosure of the indictment, the warrant of arrest, and the order for transfer and detention, and the decision approving the indictment, an order for non-disclosure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you'll see once again in the penultimate paragraph that learned Judge ordered, on the 12th of June, that the indictment and the warrant be made public; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Would I be correct in understanding or would you agree with me that the only -- or a reasonable conclusion for David Crane's going public on the 4th of June, 2003, that an indictment had been issued and a warrant obtained, was that as the applicant for those protective measures, it was considered he could make that fact public without a direct court order? Would you agree with that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Certainly, in the circumstances of this particular case, that was the view that was taken, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Now, if you could go to tab 12 of the file. And just one moment. I should ask : There was never at any stage any allegations of contempt against Mr. David Crane, was there, for going public on the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: No, there wasn't, but certainly there were -- there were, I think, seen to be extenuating circumstances so far as that particular action was concerned. And he was an officer of the court. I'm sorry, tab 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And garbed as David Crane was with the role of high office, being the Prosecutor, did that give him some particular special authorities in relation to an order of the judiciary that a member of the public would not enjoy? Is that what you're saying, Mr. Vincent?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: What I'm saying is, is that as I recall the circumstances, that the opportunity for the indictment to be served, and other details, presented itself unexpectedly and very late around that time. I can't be precise whether it was the 3rd of June or the 4th of June, but certainly as will you will probably know, that was on the information having been provided to the Prosecutor that the person, the subject of the indictment and the arrest warrant, had, in fact, for the first time left his own country, and the Prosecutor felt that he had to act in the best interests. What contact he had -- emergency contact he had with the Judge of the Trial Chamber, I was not aware, but I was instructed to serve the papers on the respective diplomatic officials that evening and the following morning to coincide with the person who was subject to that order arriving in a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vincent, I don't want to delay you too long. I'm not asking you about your own conduct, and forgive me if I wasn't clear. Let me go back to the question. Is it your contention to Their Honours that the official position of an individual as a Prosecutor gives him particular rights, vis-a-vis orders of the Bench, that members of the public do not enjoy? Is that your contention, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Certainly. Can I say straightaway that I wasn't attempting to defend my conduct. The situation was that in the circumstances, I believed that he had the authority to do that, in the particular circumstances, in the best interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And one of the reasons motivating you to that conclusion, perhaps, is the fact that as the applicant for those protective measures, he could decide that those measures were no longer necessary, albeit in the interests of - how did you put it - in the interest -- in the best interests of justice?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Can we go to tab 12, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: I'm at tab 12, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Can you see that document? It's a CNN news report.

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And can you see that CNN's Christiane Amanpour stated that: "An indictment in relation to Slobodan Milosevic is likely to be handed down this week, perhaps as early as Thursday. Details on the indictment are not available. Other people may be named. The Tribunal would not comment on the report?" Do you have any knowledge of the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Only that which I picked up from press reports and also somewhat belatedly after I was here for five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And would it be a fair conclusion, from reading this report, that perhaps Christiane Amanpour made public that an indictment was imminent before the indictment had been publicly made available by the Court? Is that a fair reading of the news report?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: With respect, no, I don't think it is. I think it's pure speculation, and speculation is rife around all the international courts and tribunals. And I think for every press release that you will show me, I could probably give you 10 or 15 which happens around the Lebanon Tribunal in the last three months, none of which have had any factual base or accuracy, but have been pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, bear with me for a moment. You see the second paragraph -- are you familiar with Christiane Amanpour in your work as Registrar of various courts?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Yes, I have met her, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that she is one of the most well-respected commentators on the news media?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: I think that's a fair assessment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: She's not an individual given for wild conjecture, is she, in your experience?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: No. But with experience, of course, comes, perhaps, a better understanding of the events within tribunals. But with the greatest of respect, whether she is experienced or otherwise, my reading of this is it's speculation. I mean, the word "likely" gives that away, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And if you see in paragraph 2, the speculation seems to be quite specific, because she states that the indictment is likely to be handed -- "is likely to be handed down this week, perhaps as early as Thursday."

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It's quite specific speculation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Well, speculation comes in a series of forms, but "likely" is still, as far as I'm concerned, the word that actually controls all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And if I told you that the indictment, indeed, did come down, was made public in that week, would you think perhaps that it would make the report accurate, would it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: It certainly would do, but as I understand, tribunals don't normally go through a series where they look at speculation and then tick a box whether it's right or wrong. I suspect that probably, in your distinguished career, you'll come across many such press reports which have subsequently disappeared and sunk without trace and have never proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: But in this particular case, in this particular case, if you had been the Registrar at the time, would any alarm bells have sounded from this report?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: If I had been Registrar at the time, one is always concerned about speculation if it appears from your knowledge to have some basis of truth, but the situation is, as I say, again based on my experience, I have reached the stage where I have become, to a certain extent, somewhat kind of cynical with reporting from the press in a number of respects, so you read it as it is. I think if there is -- if there was details which actually talked about names, events, et cetera, then I would be concerned that there would have been a breach of confidentiality, and I would have perhaps looked internally to see where it might have come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you can see, of course, in the first paragraph the name Slobodan Milosevic is mentioned; you can see that, can you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If you go to the second page, it's another CNN news report, and it states much the same thing, but what it adds is that the Tribunal would not comment on the report, but would hold a news conference "on Thursday."

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And it gives these details. So these types of reports were commonplace; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: Yes. I think they are in my experience of all the tribunals, there is a -- there is a huge -- and it's a phrase I'm not sure exactly that it covers the issue, but known as the "feeding frenzy," so far as the press are concerned. And there is always a significant amount of speculation, but there is in life generally, and just eventually somebody gets it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. So you think with Christiane Amanpour, it was just potluck?

utterances.speaker: ROBIN VINCENT.
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's potluck, but, I mean, you, yourself, referred to her experience, and that is why she's respected. I mean, she certainly has a significant understanding amongst the international press of events, and so, therefore, it's not unusual sometimes that things -- people can put 2 and 2 together and actually make 4 or 5, and so, no, it doesn't come as any surprise to me, and it's fairly commonplace in these tribunals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
